Equation (60) is the well-known Lindhard dielectric matrix, and the diagonal matrix elements are the same as in Eq. (4) (see Mahan, 1993, and Giuliani and Vignale, 2005, for in-depth discussions of the Lindhard function). By following the same steps that led to Eq. (58), replacing the bare ionic potential by its screened counterpart, and using Eq. (53) with ϵ\epsilon instead of ϵH​x​c\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}, we obtain:

gm​n​ν(𝐤,𝐪)=−i[ℏ/(2NpMκω𝐪​ν)]12𝐪⋅𝐞κ,ν(𝐪)Vκ(𝐪)/ϵ(q).g_{mn\nu}({\bf k},{\bf q})=-i\left[\hbar/(2N_{p}M_{\kappa}\omega_{{\bf q}\nu})\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bf q}\cdot{\bf e}_{\kappa,\nu}({\bf q})\,V_{\kappa}({\bf q})/\epsilon(q). (61)

Here we considered only one atom at the center of the unit cell, and we neglected umklapp processes. This is essentially the result derived by Bardeen [38] and reproduced in Eq. (3).

IV Field-theoretic approach to the electron-phonon interaction

In Sec. III we discussed how the materials parameters entering the electron-phonon Hamiltonian in Eq. (1), namely εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n{\bf k}}, ω𝐪​ν\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}, and gm​n​ν​(𝐤,𝐪)g_{mn\nu}({\bf k},{\bf q}), can be calculated from first principles using DFT and DFPT. Today the formalism and techniques described in Sec. III constitute de facto the standard tool in quantitative studies of electron-phonon interactions in solids (see Secs. VII-XII).

However, it should be noted that the DFT approach to EPIs does not rest on strong theoretical foundations. For one, the evaluation of the EPI matrix elements via Eq. (38) relies on the assumption that the interaction between electrons and nuclei is governed by the effective Kohn-Sham potential; therefore we can expect the matrix elements to be sensitive to the exchange and correlation functional (see Sec. XII). Furthermore, the very definition of phonons starting from Eq. (12) relies on the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, and one might ask whether this choice is accurate enough in metals and narrow-gap semiconductors (see Sec. VII). Finally, if one were to go beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, then it would seem sensible to also incorporate retardation effects in the calculation of the EPI matrix elements.

On top of these practical points, and at a more fundamental level, we expect that the electron-phonon interaction will modify both the electronic structure and the lattice dynamics of a solid, and these modifications will in turn affect the coupling between electrons and phonons. It is therefore clear that a complete theory of interacting electrons and phonons must be self-consistent. In order to address these issues it is necessary to formulate the electron-phonon problem using a rigorous and general theory of interacting electrons and phonons in solids.

The most systematic and elegant approach is based on quantum field theory [364], and is tightly connected with the development of the G​WGW method [187]. The first attempts in this direction were from Nakajima [299], Bardeen and Pines [39], Migdal [286], and Engelsberg and Schrieffer [129]. However, from the point of view of the present article, these works are of limited usefulness since they were mostly developed around the homogeneous electron gas.

A completely general formulation of the problem, which seamlessly applies to metals, semiconductors, and insulators, was first provided by Baym [46] and subsequently by Hedin and Lundqvist [189]. The formalism developed in these articles constitutes today the most complete theory of the electron-phonon problem. In fact, many aspects of this formalism are yet to be explored within the context of ab initio calculations. After these seminal works several authors contributed to clarifying various aspects of the many-body theory of the coupled electron-phonon system, including Keating [216], Gillis [150], Sjölander and Johnson [372], Maksimov [268], Vogl [391], and more recently van Leeuwen [253], Marini et al. [276]. In particular, van Leeuwen focused on the issues of translational and rotational invariance of the resulting theory, while Marini et al. analyzed the connection between many-body perturbation theory approaches and DFT calculations.

Since the mathematical notation of the original articles is obsolete and rather difficult to follow, in Secs. IV.1-IV.4 we cover the theory in some detail using contemporary notation. The following derivations can be found across the works of Kato et al. [213], Baym [46], Hedin and Lundqvist [189], and Maksimov [268]. Here we provide a synthesis of these contributions using a unified notation, and we fill the gaps wherever it is necessary. The presentation requires some familiarity with field operators (see for example Merzbacher, 1998 for a succinct introduction).

IV.1 Operators and distinguishability

The starting point for studying EPIs using a field-theoretic approach is to define the Fock space and the field operators for electrons and nuclei. In the case of electrons the choice is unambiguous, since any many-body state can be represented as a linear combination of Slater determinants constructed using a basis of single-particle wavefunctions. In the case of nuclei the situation is slightly more ambiguous: in principle we might proceed in a very general way by choosing to focus on the nuclei as our quantum particles, as opposed to their displacements from equilibrium. In practice this choice leads to a dead end for two reasons. Firstly, the quantum statistics of nuclei would be dependent on their spin, therefore we would end up with an unwieldy mix of fermions and bosons depending on the solid. Secondly, the notion of ‘indistinguishable’ particles, which is central to second quantization, does not apply to nuclei in solids (at least in thermodynamic equilibrium and far from a solid-liquid phase transition). In fact, in many cases we can directly label the nuclei, for example by means of experimental probes such as scanning tunneling microscopy and electron diffraction. In order to avoid these issues, it is best to study the electron-phonon problem by considering (i) indistinguishable electrons, for which it is convenient to use second-quantized operators; (ii) distinguishable nuclei, for which it is best to use first quantization in the displacements; (iii) indistinguishable phonons, resulting from the quantization of the nuclear displacements; in this latter case the distinction between first and second quantization is irrelevant. These aspects are briefly mentioned by Baym [46] and Maksimov [268].

With these choices, the dynamical variables of the problem are the electronic field operators ψ^{\hat{\psi}} (discussed below) and the nuclear displacements from equilibrium Δ​𝝉^\Delta\hat{{\bm{\tau}}} (discussed in Sec. IV.3). In this theory the equilibrium coordinates of the nuclei are regarded as external parameters, and are to be obtained for example from crystallography or DFT calculations. Throughout this section, we limit ourselves to consider equilibrium Green’s functions at zero temperature. As a result, all expectation values will be evaluated for the electron-nuclei ground state |0⟩|0\rangle. The extension of the main results to finite temperature is presented in Sec. V. We will not specify how to obtain the ground state, since the following discussion is independent on the precise shape of this state. In order to derive expressions that are useful for first-principles calculations, at the very end the ground state will be approximated using standard DFT wavefunctions and phonons (see Sec. V).

The electronic field creation/destruction operators are denoted by ψ^†​(𝐱){\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x})/ψ^​(𝐱){\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}), where the variable 𝐱{\bf x} indicates both the position 𝐫{\bf r} and the spin label σ\sigma. These operators obey the anti-commutation relations [285]: {ψ^​(𝐱),ψ^​(𝐱′)}={ψ^†​(𝐱),ψ^†​(𝐱′)}=0\{{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}),{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}^{\prime})\}\!=\!\{{\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}),{\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}^{\prime})\}\!=\!0, {ψ^​(𝐱),ψ^†​(𝐱′)}=δ⁡(𝐱−𝐱′)\{{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}),{\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}^{\prime})\}=\delta({\bf x}\!-\!{\bf x}^{\prime}). The most general non-relativistic Hamiltonian for a system of coupled electrons and nuclei can be written as:

H^=T^e+T^n+U^ee+U^nn+U^en,{\hat{H}}={\hat{T}}_{\rm e}+{\hat{T}}_{\rm n}+{\hat{U}}_{\rm ee}+{\hat{U}}_{\rm nn}+{\hat{U}}_{\rm en}, (62)

where each term will be introduced hereafter. The electron kinetic energy is:

T^e=−ℏ22​me∫d𝐱ψ^†(𝐱)∇2ψ^(𝐱),{\hat{T}}_{\rm e}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\int\!d{\bf x}\,{\hat{\psi}}^{\dagger}({\bf x})\,\nabla^{2}\,{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}), (63)

with mem_{\rm e} being the electron mass, and the integrals ∫𝑑𝐱\int\!d{\bf x} denoting the sum over spin and the integration over space, ∑σ∫𝑑𝐫{\sum}_{\sigma}\!\int d{\bf r}. The electron-electron interaction is:

U^ee=12​∫d​𝐫​∫d​𝐫′​n^e​(𝐫)​[n^e​(𝐫′)−δ⁡(𝐫−𝐫′)]​v​(𝐫,𝐫′),{\hat{U}}_{\rm ee}=\frac{1}{2}\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}\!\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\left[{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r}^{\prime})-\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime})\right]v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}), (64)

where the electron particle density operator is given by n^e​(𝐫)=∑σψ^†​(𝐱)​ψ^​(𝐱){\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})={\sum}_{\sigma}{\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}){\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}), and where v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=e2/(4​π​ε0​|𝐫−𝐫′|)v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})=e^{2}/(4\pi\varepsilon_{0}|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|) is the Coulomb interaction between two particles of charge ee. In Eqs. (63) and (64) the integrals are over the entire crystal. This corresponds to considering a supercell of infinite size (therefore the lattice vectors 𝐓{\bf T} of the supercell drop out) and a dense sampling of wavevectors 𝐪{\bf q} in the Brillouin zone. This choice is useful in order to maintain the formalism as light as possible. Accordingly, all sums over 𝐪{\bf q} are replaced using Np−1∑𝐪→ΩBZ−1∫d𝐪N_{p}^{-1}{\sum}_{\bf q}\rightarrow\Omega_{\rm BZ}^{-1}\int\!d{\bf q}, where the integral is over the Brillouin zone of volume ΩBZ\Omega_{\rm BZ}. Similarly the closure relations in Eq. (213) are replaced by: ∫d​𝐪​exp⁡(i​𝐪⋅𝐑p)=ΩBZ​δp​0\int\!d{\bf q}\exp(i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}_{p})=\Omega_{\rm BZ}\,\delta_{p0} and ∑pexp⁡(i​𝐪⋅𝐑p)=ΩBZ​δ​(𝐪)\sum_{p}\exp(i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}_{p})=\Omega_{\rm BZ}\,\delta({\bf q}). The nuclear kinetic energy operator is the same as the last term in Eq. (19). Using the same notation as in Sec. III the nucleus-nucleus interaction energy is:

U^nn=12​∑κ′​p′≠κ​pZκ​Zκ′​v​(𝝉κ​p0+Δ​𝝉^κ​p,𝝉κ′​p′0+Δ​𝝉^κ′​p′).{\hat{U}}_{\rm nn}=\frac{1}{2}\!\!\sum_{\,\,\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}\neq\kappa p}Z_{\kappa}Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}v({\bm{\tau}}^{0}_{\kappa p}+\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p},{\bm{\tau}}^{0}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}+\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}). (65)

Here 𝝉κ​p0{\bm{\tau}}^{0}_{\kappa p} denotes the classical equilibrium position of each nucleus, and the displacement operators Δ​𝝉^κ​p\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p} will later be expressed in terms of the ladder operators from Appendix B. The electron-nucleus interaction energy is:

U^en=∫d​𝐫​∫d​𝐫′​n^e​(𝐫)​n^n​(𝐫′)​v​(𝐫,𝐫′),{\hat{U}}_{\rm en}=\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}\!\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r}){\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}^{\prime})v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}), (66)

where the nuclear charge density operator is given by:

n^n(𝐫)=−∑κ​pZκδ(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0−Δ𝝉^κ​p).{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r})=-{\sum}_{\kappa p}Z_{\kappa}\,\delta({\bf r}-{\bm{\tau}}^{0}_{\kappa p}-\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}). (67)

Here the density operators are expressed in units of the electron charge, so that the expectation value of the total charge density is −e​⟨0|​n^​(𝐫)​|0⟩-e\langle 0|{\hat{n}}({\bf r})|0\rangle with n^​(𝐫)=n^e​(𝐫)+n^n​(𝐫){\hat{n}}({\bf r})={\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})+{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}).

We underline the asymmetry between Eqs. (64) and (65): in the case of electrons one considers the electrostatic energy of a continuous distribution of charge, and the unphysical self-interaction is removed by the Dirac delta; whereas in the case of nuclei, the particles are distinguishable therefore one has to take into account all pairwise interactions individually.

IV.2 Electron Green’s function

IV.2.1 Equation of motion and self-energy

In this section we focus on the electrons. By combining Eqs. (62)-(66) and using the anti-commutation relations for the field operators one finds the standard expression:

H^\displaystyle{\hat{H}} =\displaystyle= T^n+U^nn+∫d​𝐱​ψ^†​(𝐱)​[−ℏ22​me​∇2+V^n​(𝐫)]​ψ^​(𝐱)\displaystyle{\hat{T}}_{\rm n}+{\hat{U}}_{\rm nn}+\int\!d{\bf x}\,{\hat{\psi}}^{\dagger}({\bf x})\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}+\hat{V}_{\rm n}({\bf r})\right]{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}) (68)
+\displaystyle+ 12​∫d​𝐱​d​𝐱′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ψ^†​(𝐱)​ψ^†​(𝐱′)​ψ^​(𝐱′)​ψ^​(𝐱),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\!\!d{\bf x}\,d{\bf x}^{\prime}\,v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}){\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}){\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}^{\prime}){\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}^{\prime}){\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}),

where the nuclear potential V^n\hat{V}_{\rm n} is given by:

V^n​(𝐫)=∫d​𝐫′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​n^n​(𝐫′).\hat{V}_{\rm n}({\bf r})=\int\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}){\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}^{\prime}). (69)

In order to study the excitation spectrum of the many-body Hamiltonian H^{\hat{H}} at equilibrium we need to determine the time-ordered one-electron Green’s function (Kato et al., 1960; Fetter and Walecka, 2003). At zero temperature this function is defined as:

G⁡(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)=−iℏ​⟨0|T^​ψ​(𝐱​t)​ψ†​(𝐱′​t′)|0⟩,G({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle 0|\,{\hat{T}}\,\psi({\bf x}t)\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})|0\rangle, (70)

where T^{\hat{T}} is Wick’s time-ordering operator for fermions, and ensures that the times of the subsequent operators increase towards the left. The formal definition of the Wick operator is: T^​ψ​(𝐱​t)​ψ†​(𝐱′​t′)=θ⁡(t−t′)​ψ​(𝐱​t)​ψ†​(𝐱′​t′)−θ⁡(t′−t)​ψ†​(𝐱′​t′)​ψ​(𝐱​t){\hat{T}}\psi({\bf x}t)\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})=\theta(t\!-\!t^{\prime})\psi({\bf x}t)\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})-\theta(t^{\prime}\!-\!t)\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})\psi({\bf x}t), where θ\theta is the Heaviside function. Based on this definition we see that for t>t′t>t^{\prime} the Green’s function in Eq. (70) corresponds to the scalar product between the initial state ψ†​(𝐱′​t′)​|0⟩\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})|0\rangle and the final state ψ†​(𝐱​t)​|0⟩\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}t)|0\rangle. This product is precisely the probability amplitude for finding an electron in the position 𝐱{\bf x} at the time tt, after having introduced an electron in 𝐱′{\bf x}^{\prime} at an earlier time t′t^{\prime}. In the case t<t′t<t^{\prime} the situation is reversed and the Green’s function describes the propagation of a hole created in the system at the time t′t^{\prime}.

In order to determine G⁡(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)G({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime}) we need to establish an equation of motion for the field operators. This can be done by describing the time-dependence of the operators within the Heisenberg picture:

ψ^(𝐱t)=ei​t​H^/ℏψ^(𝐱)e−itH^/ℏ,{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t)=e^{it{\hat{H}}/\hbar}\,{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x})\,e^{-it{\hat{H}}/\hbar}, (71)

where H^{\hat{H}} was defined in Eq. (68). From this definition it follows immediately:

i​ℏ​∂∂t​ψ^​(𝐱​t)=[ψ^​(𝐱​t),H^].i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t)=[{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t),{\hat{H}}]. (72)

By combining Eqs. (68) and (72) and using the anti-commutation relations for the field operators one obtains:

i​ℏ​∂∂t​ψ^​(𝐱​t)=[−ℏ22​me​∇2+∫d​𝐫′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​n^​(𝐫′​t)]​ψ^​(𝐱​t),i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t)=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}+\int\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\,{\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime}t)\right]{\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t), (73)

where the time-dependence in n^​(𝐫′​t){\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime}t) is to be understood in the Heisenberg sense, as in Eq. (71). This equation of motion allows us to write the corresponding equation for the electron Green’s function in Eq. (70):

[i​ℏ​∂∂t+ℏ22​me​∇2−φ⁡(𝐫​t)]​G​(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)=δ⁡(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)\displaystyle\left[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}-\varphi({\bf r}t)\right]G({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})=\delta({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})
−iℏ∫d𝐫′′dt′′v(𝐫t,𝐫′′t′′)⟨T^n^(𝐫′′t′′)ψ(𝐱t)ψ†(𝐱′t′)⟩.\displaystyle-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int\!\!d{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}dt^{\prime\prime}v({\bf r}t,{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\langle{\hat{T}}\,{\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\psi({\bf x}t)\psi^{\dagger}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})\rangle.\hskip 5.69046pt (74)

Here v⁡(𝐫​t,𝐫′′​t′′)=v⁡(𝐫,𝐫′′)​δ​(t−t′′)v({\bf r}t,{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})=v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime\prime})\delta(t-t^{\prime\prime}), the brakets ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle are a short-hand notation for ⟨0|⋯|0⟩\langle 0|\cdots|0\rangle, and the additional term φ\varphi is discussed below. In order to obtain Eq. (74) we used once again the anti-commutation relations, and we noted that the derivative of the Heaviside function is a Dirac delta.

The new term φ⁡(𝐫​t)\varphi({\bf r}t) which appeared in Eq. (74) is a scalar electric potential which couples to both electronic and nuclear charges. This potential has been introduced in order to perturb the system via the additional Hamiltonian H^1​(t)=∫d​𝐫​n^​(𝐫​t)​φ​(𝐫​t){\hat{H}}_{1}(t)=\int d{\bf r}\,{\hat{n}}({\bf r}t)\varphi({\bf r}t). The physical idea behind this choice is to use φ⁡(𝐫​t)\varphi({\bf r}t) in order to induce forced oscillations in the system. When the system resonates with the perturbation we know that the resonant frequency must correspond to a free oscillation, that is a many-body eigenmode. From a formal point of view, the potential φ⁡(𝐫​t)\varphi({\bf r}t) is introduced in order to exploit Schwinger’s functional derivative technique (Kato, 1960, Appendix II) and is set to zero at the end of the derivation.

One complication arising from the introduction of φ⁡(𝐫​t)\varphi({\bf r}t) in Eq. (74) is that the time evolution in Eq. (71) is no longer valid, since the perturbed Hamiltonian now depends on the time variable. The way around this complication is to switch from the Heisenberg picture to the interaction picture. This change amounts to replacing the exponentials in Eq. (71) by the time-ordered Dyson series U^(t)=T^exp(−iℏ−1∫0tH^(t′)dt′){\hat{U}}(t)={\hat{T}}\exp\left(-i\hbar^{-1}\int_{0}^{t}{\hat{H}}(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}\right) (Fetter and Walecka, 2003, p. 57). Since this would lead to an overlong derivation, we prefer to leave this aspect aside and refer the reader to Aryasetiawan and Gunnarsson [32] for a more comprehensive discussion.

In order to write Eq. (74) in a manageable form, we use the identity [213]:

δ⁡⟨T^​a^​(t1)​b^​(t2)⟩δ​φ​(𝐫′′​t′′)=−iℏ​⟨T^​[n^​(𝐫′′​t′′)−⟨n^​(𝐫′′​t′′)⟩]​a^​(t1)​b^​(t2)⟩.\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{T}}\hat{a}(t_{1})\hat{b}(t_{2})\rangle}{\delta\varphi({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})}\!=\!-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\!\left[{\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\rangle\right]\hat{a}(t_{1})\hat{b}(t_{2})\rangle. (75)

In this and the following expressions δ/δ​φ​(𝐫′′​t′′)\delta/\delta\varphi({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime}) denotes the functional derivative with respect to φ⁡(𝐫′′​t′′)\varphi({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime}), and should not be confused with the Dirac delta functions δ⁡(𝐱​t,𝐱′​t′)\delta({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime}). Equation (75) is proven by Kato et al. (1960, Appendix II) and by Hedin and Lundqvist (1969, Appendix B.a). After identifying a^\hat{a} and b^\hat{b} with ψ^​(𝐱​t){\hat{\psi}}({\bf x}t) and ψ^†​(𝐱′​t′){\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}}({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime}), respectively, Eq. (74) becomes:

[iℏ∂∂t+ℏ22​me∇2−Vtot(𝐫t)−iℏ∫d𝐫′′dt′′v(𝐫t+η,𝐫′′t′′)\displaystyle\,\,\left[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}-V_{\rm tot}({\bf r}t)\!-\!i\hbar\!\!\int d{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}dt^{\prime\prime}v({\bf r}t+\eta,{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\right.
×δδ​φ​(𝐫′′​t′′)]G(𝐱t,𝐱′t′)=δ(𝐱t,𝐱′t′),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\left.\times\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})}\right]G({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime})=\delta({\bf x}t,{\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime}), (76)

where η\eta is a positive infinitesimal arising from the time-ordering, and Vtot​(𝐫​t)V_{\rm tot}({\bf r}t) is the total potential acting on the electronic and nuclear charges, averaged over the many-body quantum state |0⟩|0\rangle:

Vtot​(𝐫​t)=∫d​𝐫′​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)​⟨n^​(𝐫′​t)⟩+φ⁡(𝐫​t).V_{\rm tot}({\bf r}t)=\int\!\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\langle{\hat{n}}({\bf r}^{\prime}t)\rangle+\varphi({\bf r}t). (77)

Equation (76) was first derived by Kato et al. [213]. In order to avoid a proliferation of variables, it is common practice to replace the letters by integer numbers, using the convention (𝐱​t)({\bf x}t) or (𝐫​t)→1({\bf r}t)\rightarrow 1, (𝐱′​t′)({\bf x}^{\prime}t^{\prime}) or (𝐫′​t′)→2({\bf r}^{\prime}t^{\prime})\rightarrow 2, (𝐫​t+η)→1+({\bf r}t\!+\!\eta)\rightarrow 1^{+}, and so on. Using this convention the last two equations become:

[iℏ∂∂t1+ℏ22​me∇2(1)−Vtot(1)\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt\left[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t_{1}}+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}(1)-V_{\rm tot}(1)\!\right.
−iℏ∫d3v(1+3)δδ​φ​(3)]G(12)=δ(12),\displaystyle\hskip 14.22636pt\left.-i\hbar\!\!\int d3\,v(1^{+}3)\frac{\delta}{\delta\varphi(3)}\right]G(12)=\delta(12), (78)

and

Vtot​(1)=∫d​2​v​(12)​⟨n^​(2)⟩+φ⁡(1).V_{\rm tot}(1)=\int\!\!d2\,v(12)\langle{\hat{n}}(2)\rangle+\varphi(1). (79)

In these expressions the spin labels are implied for the Green’s function and for the Dirac delta.

At this point, a set of self-consistent equations for coupled electrons and phonons can be generated by eliminating the functional derivative in Eq. (78). For this purpose one first relates the total screened electrostatic potential VtotV_{\rm tot} to the external potential φ\varphi by introducing the inverse dielectric matrix ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1} as a functional derivative:

ϵ−1​(12)=δ​Vtot​(1)/δ​φ​(2).\epsilon^{-1}(12)=\delta V_{\rm tot}(1)\,/\,\delta\varphi(2). (80)

The function ϵ−1​(12)\epsilon^{-1}(12) is the many-body counterpart of the dielectric matrix discussed in Sec. III.2.4. The form given by Eq. (80) is the most general field-theoretic formulation for a system of interacting electrons and nuclei.

The next step is to rewrite δ​G/δ​φ\delta G/\delta\varphi inside Eq. (78) in terms of the inverse Green’s function, G−1G^{-1}. By using the fact that δ​∫d​2​G​(12)​G−1​(23)=0\delta\int d2\,G(12)\,G^{-1}(23)=0 and the rule for the functional derivative of a product [210] one obtains:

δ​G​(12)δ​φ​(3)=−∫d(45)G(14)δ​G−1​(45)δ​φ​(3)G(52).\frac{\delta G(12)}{\delta\varphi(3)}=-\!\int\!d(45)G(14)\frac{\delta G^{-1}(45)}{\delta\varphi(3)}G(52). (81)

In order to eliminate any explicit reference to φ\varphi we can express the functional derivative on the right-hand side using the chain rule for functional differentiation [210]:

δ​G−1​(45)δ​φ​(3)=∫d​6​δ​G−1​(45)δ​Vtot​(6)​δ​Vtot​(6)δ​φ​(3).\frac{\delta G^{-1}(45)}{\delta\varphi(3)}=\int d6\frac{\delta G^{-1}(45)}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(6)}\frac{\delta V_{\rm tot}(6)}{\delta\varphi(3)}. (82)

It is customary to call ‘vertex’ the three-point quantity defined by:

Γ(123)=−δG−1(12)/δVtot(3).\Gamma(123)=-\,\delta G^{-1}(12)\,/\,\delta V_{\rm tot}(3). (83)

By combining Eqs. (78) and (80)-(83) one finds:

[i​ℏ​∂∂t1+ℏ22​me​∇2(1)−Vtot​(1)]​G​(12)\displaystyle\hskip-28.45274pt\left[i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t_{1}}+\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m_{\rm e}}\nabla^{2}(1)-V_{\rm tot}(1)\right]G(12)
−∫d3Σ(13)G(32)=δ(12),\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt-\int\!\!d3\,\Sigma(13)\,G(32)=\delta(12), (84)

having introduced the so-called ‘electron self-energy’ Σ\Sigma:

Σ⁡(12)=i​ℏ​∫d⁡(34)​G​(13)​Γ​(324)​W​(41+),\Sigma(12)=i\hbar\int\!\!d(34)G(13)\Gamma(324)W(41^{+}), (85)

which in turn contains the ‘screened Coulomb interaction’ WW, defined as:

W⁡(12)=∫d​3​ϵ−1​(13)​v​(32)=∫d⁡(3)​v​(13)​ϵ−1​(23).W(12)=\!\int\!\!d3\,\epsilon^{-1}(13)\,v(32)=\!\int\!\!d(3)\,v(13)\epsilon^{-1}(23).\!\! (86)

The last equality can be obtained by observing that δ⁡⟨n^​(1)⟩/δ​φ​(2)=δ⁡⟨n^​(2)⟩/δ​φ​(1)\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(1)\rangle/\delta\varphi(2)=\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(2)\rangle/\delta\varphi(1) after Eq. (75), therefore W⁡(12)=W⁡(21)W(12)=W(21).

Now, by inverting Eq. (84) and using Eq. (83), we can express the vertex Γ\Gamma in terms of Σ\Sigma and GG:

Γ⁡(123)=δ⁡(12)​δ​(13)+∫d⁡(4567)​δ​Σ​(12)δ​G​(45)​G​(46)​G​(75)​Γ​(673).\Gamma(123)\!=\!\delta(12)\delta(13)+\!\int\!\!d(4567)\frac{\delta\Sigma(12)}{\delta G(45)}G(46)G(75)\Gamma(673). (87)

The derivation of this result is rather lengthy: it requires the use of the chain rule, in symbols δ/δ​Vtot=(δ​G/δ​Vtot)​δ/δ​G\delta/\delta V_{\rm tot}=(\delta G/\delta V_{\rm tot})\delta/\delta G, as well as Eq. (81) with Σ\Sigma and VtotV_{\rm tot} instead of GG and φ\varphi, respectively.

Equations (84)-(87) form a nonlinear system of equations for the electron Green’s function, GG, the electron self-energy, Σ\Sigma, the total screened Coulomb interaction, WW, and the vertex, Γ\Gamma. In order to close the loop it remains to specify the relation between WW and the other quantities. The next section is devoted to this aspect.

IV.2.2 The screened Coulomb interaction

An equation for the screened Coulomb interaction can be found by combining Eqs. (79), (80), and (86):

W⁡(12)=v⁡(12)+∫d⁡(34)​v​(13)​δ​⟨n^​(3)⟩δ​Vtot​(4)​W​(42).W(12)=v(12)+\!\int\!d(34)\,v(13)\,\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(3)\rangle}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(4)}\,W(42). (88)

By defining the ‘polarization propagator’ as:

P⁡(12)=δ​⟨n^​(1)⟩δ​Vtot​(2),P(12)=\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(2)}, (89)

the previous expression takes the usual form [187]:

W⁡(12)=v⁡(12)+∫d⁡(34)​v​(13)​P​(34)​W​(42).W(12)=v(12)+\!\int\!d(34)\,v(13)P(34)W(42). (90)

This result can be combined with Eq. (86) in order to express the dielectric matrix in terms of the polarization:

ϵ⁡(12)=δ⁡(12)−∫d⁡(3)​v​(13)​P​(32).\epsilon(12)=\delta(12)-\!\int\!\!d(3)v(13)P(32). (91)

We now consider the special case whereby the nuclei are regarded as classical point charges clamped to their equilibrium positions. In this situation, the variation of the charge density δ​⟨n^⟩\delta\langle{\hat{n}}\rangle in Eq. (89) corresponds to the re-distribution of the electronic charge in response to the perturbation δ​Vtot\delta V_{\rm tot}. In order to describe this special case it is convenient to introduce a new polarization propagator, PeP_{\rm e}, associated with the electronic response only:

Pe(12)=δ​⟨n^e​(1)⟩δ​Vtot​(2)=−iℏ∑σ1∫d(34)G(13)G(41+)Γ(342).P_{\rm e}(12)=\!\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}_{\rm e}(1)\rangle}{\delta V_{\rm tot}(2)}=\!-i\hbar\!\sum_{\sigma_{1}}\!\!\int\!d(34)G(13)G(41^{+})\Gamma(342). (92)

The last equality in this expression is obtained by using Eq. (81) with VtotV_{\rm tot} instead of φ\varphi, together with Eq. (83), and by considering that the electron density is related to the Green’s function via the relation:

⟨n^e(1)⟩=−iℏ∑σ1G(11+).\langle{\hat{n}}_{\rm e}(1)\rangle=-i\hbar{\sum}_{\sigma_{1}}G(11^{+}). (93)

In conjunction with PeP_{\rm e} it is natural to define the Coulomb interaction screened by the electronic polarization only:

We​(12)=v⁡(12)+∫d⁡(34)​v​(13)​Pe​(34)​We​(42),W_{\rm e}(12)=v(12)+\!\int\!d(34)\,v(13)P_{\rm e}(34)W_{\rm e}(42), (94)

as well as the associated dielectric matrix, in analogy with Eq. (91):

ϵe​(12)=δ⁡(12)−∫d​3​v​(13)​Pe​(32).\epsilon_{\rm e}(12)=\delta(12)-\!\int\!d3\,v(13)P_{\rm e}(32). (95)

Taken together, Eqs. (84)-(87) with WW replaced by WeW_{\rm e} constitute the well-known Hedin’s equations for a system of interacting electrons when the nuclei are clamped to their equilibrium positions [187].

In order to go back to the most general case whereby the nuclei are not clamped to their equilibrium positions, one has to describe the re-adjustment of both electronic and nuclear charge. To this aim we combine Eq. (80), (86), (88), (92), (94), and (95). The result is:

W⁡(12)=We​(12)+∫d⁡(34)​We​(13)​δ​⟨n^n​(3)⟩δ​φ​(4)​v​(42).W(12)=W_{\rm e}(12)+\!\int\!d(34)\,W_{\rm e}(13)\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(3)\rangle}{\delta\varphi(4)}v(42). (96)

An explicit expression for δ​⟨n^n⟩/δ​φ\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}\rangle/\delta\varphi can be obtained using the following reasoning. We go into the details since this is a delicate passage. Equation (75) provides a recipe for evaluating the variation of any operator with respect to a potential φ⁡(𝐫​t)\varphi({\bf r}t) which couples to the total charge density operator n^​(𝐫​t){\hat{n}}({\bf r}t) via H^1​(t)=∫d​𝐫​n^​(𝐫​t)​φ​(𝐫​t){\hat{H}}_{1}(t)=\int d{\bf r}\,{\hat{n}}({\bf r}t)\varphi({\bf r}t). Therefore we can replace a^​b^\hat{a}\,\hat{b} in Eq. (75) by n^n{\hat{n}_{\rm n}} to obtain:

δ​⟨n^n​(1)⟩δ​φ​(2)=−iℏ​⟨T^​[n^​(2)−⟨n^​(2)⟩]​[n^n​(1)−⟨n^n​(1)⟩]⟩.\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta\varphi(2)}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\!\left[{\hat{n}}(2)\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}}(2)\rangle\right]\![{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)-\!\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle]\rangle.\!\!\! (97)

In addition, if we introduce a second perturbation, H^2​(t)=∫d​𝐫​n^n​(𝐫​t)​J​(𝐫​t){\hat{H}}_{2}(t)=\int d{\bf r}\,{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}t)J({\bf r}t), which couples only to the nuclear charges, we can repeat the same reasoning as in Eq. (97) after replacing φ\varphi by JJ and n^{\hat{n}} by n^n{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}:

δ​⟨n^​(1)⟩δ​J​(2)=−iℏ​⟨T^​[n^n​(2)−⟨n^n​(2)⟩]​[n^​(1)−⟨n^​(1)⟩]⟩.\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta J(2)}\!=\!-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\!\left[{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\rangle\right][{\hat{n}}(1)-\langle{\hat{n}}(1)\rangle]\rangle. (98)

The comparison between Eqs. (97) and (98) yields:

δ​⟨n^n​(1)⟩δ​φ​(2)=δ​⟨n^​(2)⟩δ​J​(1).\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta\varphi(2)}=\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(2)\rangle}{\delta J(1)}. (99)

This can be restated by using the chain rule, δ​⟨n^e⟩/δ​J=\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}\rangle/\delta J= δ⁡⟨n^e⟩/δ​Vtot×δ​Vtot/δ⁡⟨n⟩×δ⁡⟨n⟩/δ​J\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}\rangle/\delta V_{\rm tot}\times\delta V_{\rm tot}/\delta\langle n\rangle\times\delta\langle n\rangle/\delta J:

δ​⟨n^​(1)⟩δ​J​(2)=∫d​3​ϵe−1​(13)​δ​⟨n^n​(3)⟩δ​J​(2).\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta J(2)}=\int\!\!d3\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)\,\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(3)\rangle}{\delta J(2)}. (100)

The variation δ​⟨n^n⟩/δ​J\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}\rangle/\delta J on the right-hand side can be expressed as in Eq. (98):

δ​⟨n^n​(1)⟩δ​J​(2)=−iℏ​⟨T^​[n^n​(2)−⟨n^n​(2)⟩]​n^n​(1)⟩,\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle}{\delta J(2)}\!=\!-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\!\left[{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\rangle\right]{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle, (101)

and since ⟨n^n−⟨n^n⟩⟩=0\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}-\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}\rangle\rangle=0 this can also be rewritten as:

δ⁡⟨n^n​(1)⟩/δ​J​(2)=D⁡(21),\delta\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle/\delta J(2)\!=\!D(21), (102)

having defined:

D⁡(12)=−iℏ​⟨T^​[n^n​(1)−⟨n^n​(1)⟩]​[n^n​(2)−⟨n^n​(2)⟩]⟩.D(12)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\!\left[{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(1)\rangle\right]\left[{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\!-\!\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}(2)\rangle\right]\rangle. (103)

This quantity is called the ‘density-density correlation function’ for the nuclei. Finally, we can combine Eqs. (96), (99), (100), and (103) to obtain:

W⁡(12)=We​(12)+Wph​(12),W(12)=W_{\rm e}(12)+W_{\rm ph}(12), (104)

where WphW_{\rm ph} is the nuclear contribution to the screened Coulomb interaction, and is given by:

Wph​(12)=∫d⁡(34)​We​(13)​D​(34)​We​(24).W_{\rm ph}(12)=\int\!\!d(34)\,W_{\rm e}(13)D(34)W_{\rm e}(24). (105)

This important result was derived first by Hedin and Lundqvist [189].

IV.2.3 Nuclear contribution to the screened Coulomb interaction

In view of the forthcoming discussion, it is useful to derive a more explicit expression for the screened interaction WphW_{\rm ph} in Eq. (105). Here we follow Baym [46], Maksimov [268]. The Taylor expansion of the Dirac delta to second order in the displacement 𝐮{\bf u} reads:

δ(𝐫−𝐮)=δ(𝐫)−𝐮⋅∇δ(𝐫)+12𝐮⋅∇∇δ(𝐫)⋅𝐮,\delta({\bf r}-{\bf u})=\delta({\bf r})-{\bf u}\cdot\nabla\delta({\bf r})+\frac{1}{2}{\bf u}\!\cdot\!\nabla\nabla\delta({\bf r})\!\cdot\!{\bf u}, (106)

where 𝐮⋅∇∇⋅𝐮{\bf u}\cdot\nabla\nabla\cdot{\bf u} is a short-hand notation for the second-order derivative ∑α​α′uα​uα′​∇α∇α′{\sum}_{{\alpha}{\alpha}^{\prime}}u_{\alpha}u_{{\alpha}^{\prime}}\nabla_{{\alpha}}\nabla_{{\alpha}^{\prime}}. The above expression derives from the Fourier representation of the Dirac delta. Using Eq. (106) inside (67) we deduce:

n^n​(𝐫)\displaystyle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= nn0​(𝐫)+∑κ​pZκ​Δ​𝝉^κ​p⋅∇δ​(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)\displaystyle n_{\rm n}^{0}({\bf r})+{\sum}_{\kappa p}Z_{\kappa}\,\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}\cdot\nabla\delta({\bf r}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0}) (107)
−\displaystyle- 12∑κ​pZκΔ𝝉^κ​p⋅∇∇δ(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)⋅Δ𝝉^κ​p,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}{\sum}_{\kappa p}Z_{\kappa}\,\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}\cdot\nabla\nabla\delta({\bf r}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0})\cdot\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,

where nn0​(𝐫)n_{\rm n}^{0}({\bf r}) is the density of nuclear point charges at the classical equilibrium positions 𝝉κ​p0\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0}. After taking into account the time evolution in the Heisenberg picture as in Eq. (71), we can replace this expansion inside Eq. (103) to obtain:

D⁡(12)=∑κ​α​pκ′​α′​p′Zκ​∇1,αδ​(𝐫1−𝝉κ​p0)​Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t1​t2)D(12)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa{\alpha}p\\ \kappa^{\prime}\!{\alpha}^{\prime}\!p^{\prime}\end{subarray}}Z_{\kappa}\nabla_{1,{\alpha}}\delta({\bf r}_{1}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0})D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t_{1}t_{2})
×Zκ′​∇2,α′δ​(𝐫2−𝝉κ′​p′0).\hskip 14.22636pt\times\,Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}\nabla_{2,{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta({\bf r}_{2}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0}). (108)

On the right-hand side we introduced the ‘displacement-displacement correlation function’:

Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)=−iℏ​⟨T^​Δ​τ^κ​α​p​(t)​Δ​τ^κ′​α′​p′​(t′)⟩.D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\langle{\hat{T}}\,\Delta\hat{\tau}_{\kappa{\alpha}p}(t)\,\Delta\hat{\tau}_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rangle. (109)

If we insert the last two equations in Eq. (105) we find:

Wph​(12)=∑κ​α​pκ′​α′​p′∫d⁡(34)​ϵe−1​(13)​∇3,αVκ​(𝐫3−𝝉κ​p0)\displaystyle W_{\rm ph}(12)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa{\alpha}p\\ \kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\int\!d(34)\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(13)\nabla_{3,{\alpha}}V_{\kappa}({\bf r}_{3}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0})
×Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t3​t4)​ϵe−1​(24)​∇4,α′Vκ′​(𝐫4−𝝉κ′​p′0).\displaystyle\times\,D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t_{3}t_{4})\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}(24)\nabla_{4,{\alpha}^{\prime}}V_{\kappa^{\prime}}({\bf r}_{4}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0}). (110)

In this expression VκV_{\kappa} is the bare Coulomb potential of a nucleus or its ionic pseudo-potential.

At this point of the derivation, Hedin and Lundqvist introduce the approximation that the electronic dielectric matrix in Eq. (110) can be replaced by its static counterpart. This choice implies the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation. In view of maintaining the formalism as general as possible, we prefer to keep retardation effects, following the earlier works by Bardeen and Pines [39] and Baym [46]. We will come back to this aspect in Secs. V.1.3 and V.2.2.

We stress that the sole approximation used until this point is to truncate the density operator for the nuclei to the second order in the atomic displacements. This is the standard harmonic approximation. Apart from this approximation, which is useful to express WphW_{\rm ph} in a tractable form, no other assumptions are made. Gillis [150] proposed a generalization of the results by Baym [46] which does not use the harmonic approximation. However, the resulting formalism is exceedingly complex, and has not been followed up.

IV.3 Phonon Green’s function

In order to complete the set of self-consistent many-body equations for the coupled electron-phonon system, it remains to specify a prescription for calculating the displacement-displacement correlation function, Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime}). This function is seldom referred to as the ‘phonon Green’s function’, even though stricly speaking this name should be reserved for the quantity −(i/ℏ)​⟨T^​a^𝐪​ν​(t)​a^𝐪′​ν′†​(t′)⟩-(i/\hbar)\langle{\hat{T}}\,{\hat{a}}_{{\bf q}\nu}(t){\hat{a}}^{\dagger}_{{\bf q}^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})\rangle which will be discussed in Sec. V.1.1. In the following we describe the procedure originally devised by Baym [46], and subsequently analyzed by Keating [216], Hedin and Lundqvist [189], Gillis [150], and Maksimov [268].

The starting point is the equation of motion for the displacement operators Δ​τ^κ​α​p​(t)\Delta\hat{\tau}_{\kappa{\alpha}p}(t). In analogy with Eq. (72) we have: iℏ∂/∂tΔ𝝉^κ​p(t)=[Δ𝝉^κ​p(t),H^]i\hbar\partial/\partial t\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}(t)=[\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}(t),{\hat{H}}]. Since we are considering the harmonic approximation and we expect the nuclei to oscillate around their equilibrium positions, it is convenient to aim for an expression resembling Newton’s equation. This can be done by taking the time-derivative of the equation of motion:

Mκ​∂2∂t2​Δ​𝝉^κ​p=−Mκℏ2​[[Δ​𝝉^κ​p,H^],H^].M_{\kappa}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}=-\frac{M_{\kappa}}{\hbar^{2}}[[\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p},{\hat{H}}],{\hat{H}}]. (111)

After evaluating the commutators using Eqs. (62)-(66) and performing the derivatives with respect to the nuclear displacements by means of Eq. (106), we obtain (the steps are laborious but straightforward):

Mκ​∂2∂t2​Δ​𝝉^κ​p​(t)=Zκ​∫d​𝐫​d​𝐫′​n^(κ​p)​(𝐫​t)​v​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle M_{\kappa}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}(t)=Z_{\kappa}\int\!\!d{\bf r}\,d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}({\bf r}t)v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})
×{−∇′δ​(𝐫′−𝝉κ​p0)+∇′[∇′δ​(𝐫′−𝝉κ​p0)⋅Δ​𝝉^κ​p​(t)]}.\displaystyle\,\,\,\times\left\{-\nabla^{\prime}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})+\nabla^{\prime}\!\left[\nabla^{\prime}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})\cdot\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}(t)\right]\!\right\}\!\!.\qquad (112)

Here n^(κ​p)​(𝐫){\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}({\bf r}) is the total charge density of electrons and nuclei, except for the contribution of the nucleus κ\kappa in the unit cell pp. In the second line ∇′\nabla^{\prime} indicates that the derivatives are taken with respect to the variable 𝐫′{\bf r}^{\prime}. At this point, we can use the functional derivative technique as in Sec. IV.2 in order to determine an expression involving the displacement-displacement correlation function from Eq. (109). Here, instead of using J⁡(𝐫)J({\bf r}) as in Sec. IV.2.2 for the nuclear density, it is convenient to work with the individual displacements, and introduce a third perturbation H^3​(t)=∑κ​p𝐅κ​p​(t)⋅Δ​𝝉^κ​p​(t){\hat{H}}_{3}(t)=\sum_{\kappa p}{\bf F}_{\kappa p}(t)\cdot\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}(t). The extra terms 𝐅κ​p​(t){\bf F}_{\kappa p}(t) have the meaning of external forces acting on the nuclei. Using this perturbation, it is possible to write the displacement-displacement correlation function in a manner similar to Eq. (101):

δ​⟨Δ​τ^κ​α​p​(t)⟩δ​Fκ′​α′​p′​(t′)=Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′).\frac{\delta\langle\Delta\hat{\tau}_{\kappa{\alpha}p}(t)\rangle}{\delta F_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})}=D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime}). (113)

This result was derived by Baym [46] using a finite-temperature formalism. As in the case of the electron Green’s function in Sec. IV.2, it can only be obtained by working in the interaction picture, and by taking into account the explicit time-dependence of the Hamiltonian H^+H^3​(t){\hat{H}}+{\hat{H}}_{3}(t). Also in the present case, we omit these details for the sake of conciseness.

If we take the expectation value of Eq. (112) in the ground state, after having added the new force term −𝐅κ​p​(t)-{\bf F}_{\kappa p}(t), and carry out the functional derivative with respect to 𝐅κ′​p′​(t′){\bf F}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime}), we obtain:

Mκ​∂2∂t2​Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)=−δκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​δ​(t​t′)\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684ptM_{\kappa}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})=-\delta_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\delta(tt^{\prime})
+Zκ∫d𝐫d𝐫′[−δ​⟨n^(κ​p)​(𝐫​t)⟩δ​Fκ′​α′​p′​(t′)v(𝐫,𝐫′)∇α′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ​p0)\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt+Z_{\kappa}\int\!\!d{\bf r}\,d{\bf r}^{\prime}\left[-\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}({\bf r}t)\rangle}{\delta F_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})}v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\nabla^{\prime}_{\!{\alpha}}\,\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}-{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})\right.
+⟨n^(κ​p)(𝐫t)⟩v(𝐫,𝐫′)∇α′∇γ′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ​p0)Dκ​γ​p,κ′​α′​p′(tt′)],\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt\left.+\langle{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}\!({\bf r}t)\rangle v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\nabla^{\prime}_{\!{\alpha}}\!\nabla^{\prime}_{\!\gamma}\,\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})D_{\kappa\gamma p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})\vphantom{\int}\right]\!\!, (114)

where the sum over the Cartesian directions γ\gamma is implied. The derivation of this result is rather cumbersome and involves the following considerations: (i) the Dirac deltas in the first line come from the force terms −𝐅κ​p-{\bf F}_{\kappa p} added to the Hamiltonian; (ii) within the Harmonic approximation the expectation value ⟨n^(κ​p)​Δ​𝝉^κ​p⟩\langle{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}\rangle can be replaced by ⟨n^(κ​p)⟩​⟨Δ​𝝉^κ​p⟩\langle{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}\rangle\langle\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}\rangle [46]; (iii) the expectation value ⟨Δ​𝝉^κ​p⟩\langle\Delta\hat{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}\rangle can be set to zero, because at the end of the derivation one sets |𝐅κ​p|=0|{\bf F}_{\kappa p}|=0 hence the expectation values of the displacements vanish. We note that Hedin and Lundqvist [189] omitted the last line of Eq. (114) in their derivation, but this term was correctly included by Baym [46] and Maksimov [268].

The remaining functional derivative in Eq. (114) can be expressed in terms of the nuclear charge density using the same strategy which led to Eq. (100). The result is:

δ​⟨n^(κ​p)​(𝐫​t)⟩δ​Fκ′​α′​p′​(t′)\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}^{(\kappa p)}({\bf r}t)\rangle}{\delta F_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})} =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐫′′​d​t′′​ϵe−1​(𝐫​t,𝐫′′​t′′)​δ⁡⟨n^n​(𝐫′′​t′′)⟩δ​Fκ′​α′​p′​(t′)\displaystyle\!\!\int\!d{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}dt^{\prime\prime}\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}({\bf r}t,{\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\frac{\delta\langle{\hat{n}}_{\rm n}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime\prime})\rangle}{\delta F_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime})} (115)
−\displaystyle- ∑γZκ​Dκ​γ​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)​∇γδ​(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0).\displaystyle\!\!{\sum}_{\gamma}Z_{\kappa}D_{\kappa\gamma p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})\nabla_{\!\gamma}\delta({\bf r}\!-\!\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0}).

By inserting this result inside Eq. (114) and using the expansion in Eq. (107), we finally obtain the equation of motion for the displacement-displacement correlation function:

Mκ​∂2∂t2​Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)=−δκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​δ​(t​t′)\displaystyle\hskip-22.76228ptM_{\kappa}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{2}}D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})=-\delta_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\delta(tt^{\prime})
−∑κ′′​α′′​p′′∫dt′′Πκ​α​p,κ′′​α′′​p′′(tt′′)Dκ′′​α′′​p′′,κ′​α′​p′(t′′t′).\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt-\!\!\!\!\sum_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}\int\!\!dt^{\prime\prime}\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}(tt^{\prime\prime})D_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime},\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(t^{\prime\prime}t^{\prime}). (116)

The quantity Πκ​p​α,κ′​p′​α′​(t​t′)\Pi_{\kappa p{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime}) in this expression is called the ‘phonon self-energy’ and is given by:

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)=\displaystyle\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})=
∫d𝐫d𝐫′[Zκ∇αδ(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)We(𝐫t,𝐫′t′)Zκ′∇α′′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ′​p′0)\displaystyle\,\,\,\,\int\!\!d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\!\left[Z_{\kappa}\nabla_{\!{\alpha}}\,\delta({\bf r}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})W_{\rm e}({\bf r}t,{\bf r}^{\prime}t^{\prime})\,Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}\nabla^{\prime}_{{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!\bm{\tau}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0})\right.
+δκ​p,κ′​p′δ(tt′)∇α⟨n^(𝐫)⟩v(𝐫,𝐫′)Zκ′∇α′′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ′​p′0)].\displaystyle\left.\hskip 20.77039pt+\,\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\delta(tt^{\prime})\,\nabla_{\alpha}\langle{\hat{n}}({\bf r})\rangle\,v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\,Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}\nabla^{\prime}_{\!{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0})\right]\!\!.
(117)

The derivation of Eq. (117) is nontrivial and is not found consistently in the literature; it requires converting the derivatives with respect to the position variables 𝐫{\bf r}, 𝐫′{\bf r}^{\prime} into derivatives with respect to the nuclear coordinates; integrating by parts in order to re-arrange the derivatives with respect to 𝐫{\bf r} and 𝐫′{\bf r}^{\prime}; invoking the harmonic approximation; and considering that, after setting the forces 𝐅k​p​(t)=0{\bf F}_{kp}(t)=0 and the field φ⁡(𝐫​t)=0\varphi({\bf r}t)=0 at the end, the expectation value ⟨n^​(𝐫​t)⟩\langle{\hat{n}}({\bf r}t)\rangle does not depend on time. The term in the third line of Eq. (117) is what Baym [46] called the ‘static force’, since it arises from the forces experienced by the nuclei in their equilibrium configuration.

In order to simplify Eq. (117) it is convenient to move from the time to the frequency domain. We use the following convention for the Fourier transform of a function f⁡(t)f(t): f⁡(ω)=∫−∞∞d​t​f​(t)​ei​ω​tf(\omega)\!=\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dtf(t)e^{i\omega t}. Since we are considering equilibrium properties in absence of time-dependent external potentials, the time variables enter in the above quantities only as differences [1]; for example We​(𝐫​t,𝐫′​t′)=We​(𝐫,𝐫′,t−t′)W_{\rm e}({\bf r}t,{\bf r}^{\prime}t^{\prime})=W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},t-t^{\prime}). As a consequence, Eq. (116) is rewritten as:

∑κ′′​α′′​p′′[Mκ​ω2​δκ​α​p,κ′′​α′′​p′′−Πκ​α​p,κ′′​α′′​p′′​(ω)]\displaystyle\hskip-22.76228pt{\sum}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}\left[M_{\kappa}\omega^{2}\delta_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}-\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}(\omega)\right]
×Dκ′′​α′′​p′′,κ′​α′​p′​(ω)=δκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′,\displaystyle\hskip 22.76228pt\times\,D_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime},\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega)=\delta_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}, (118)

whereas the phonon self-energy in the frequency-domain at equilibrium reads:

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′(ω)=∫d𝐫d𝐫′[Zκ∇αδ(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)We(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\displaystyle\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega)=\int\!\!d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\!\left[Z_{\kappa}\nabla_{\!{\alpha}}\,\delta({\bf r}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})\,W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)\right.
+δκ​p,κ′​p′∇α⟨n^(𝐫)⟩v(𝐫,𝐫′)]Zκ′∇α′′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ′​p′0).\displaystyle\hskip 8.5359pt\left.+\,\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\nabla_{\alpha}\langle{\hat{n}}({\bf r})\rangle\,v({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})\,\right]Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}\nabla^{\prime}_{\!{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0}). (119)

The second line in this expression is conveniently rewritten by making use of the acoustic sum rule. This sum rule is well-known in the theory of lattice dynamics of crystals [59], and can be generalized to the case of many-body Green’s function approaches as follows [189]:

∑κ′​p′Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(ω=0)=0​ for any ​α,α′.{\sum}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega=0)=0\,\,\mbox{ for any }\,{\alpha},{\alpha}^{\prime}. (120)

This relation was first derived by Baym [46] by imposing the condition that the nuclei in the crystal must remain near their equilibrium positions due to fictitious restoring forces. Physically this condition corresponds to considering a crystal which is held fixed in the laboratory reference frame. In this approach, the crystal cannot translate or rotate as a whole. Similar relations were derived by Sjölander and Johnson (1965) and Gillis (1970).

If we combine Eqs. (119) and (120), perform integrations by parts, and carry out the integrations in 𝐫{\bf r} and 𝐫′{\bf r}^{\prime} we obtain:

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(ω)=∑κ′′​p′′Zκ​Zκ′′​∂2∂rα​∂rα′′|𝐫=𝝉κ​p0,𝐫′=𝝉κ′′​p′′0\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega)=\sum_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}Z_{\kappa}Z_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}}\left.\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial r_{\alpha}\partial r^{\prime}_{{\alpha}^{\prime}}}\right|_{{{\bf r}\,\,={\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0},{\bf r}^{\prime}={\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}^{0}}}\!\!\!\!\!
[δκ′​p′,κ′′​p′′​We​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)−δκ​p,κ′​p′​We​(𝐫,𝐫′,0)],\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\Big[\delta_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)-\!\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},0)\Big], (121)

which fulfils the sum rule in Eq. (120).

Eqs. (118) and (121) completely define the nuclear dynamics in the harmonic approximation. After obtaining the displacement-displacement correlation function Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′​(t​t′)D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime}) by solving this set of equations, it is possible to construct the expectation value of the nuclear density using Eqs. (107) and (109):

⟨n^n​(𝐫​t)⟩=nn0​(𝐫)−i​ℏ2​∑κ​p,α​α′Zκ​∂2δ⁡(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)∂rα​∂rα′​Dκ​α​p,κ​α′​p​(t+​t).\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm n}}({\bf r}t)\rangle=n_{\rm n}^{0}({\bf r})\!-\!\frac{i\hbar}{2}\!\!\sum_{\kappa p,{\alpha}{\alpha}^{\prime}}\!\!Z_{\kappa}\frac{\partial^{2}\delta({\bf r}-\bm{\tau}_{\kappa p}^{0})}{\partial r_{\alpha}\partial r_{{\alpha}^{\prime}}}D_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa{\alpha}^{\prime}p}(t^{+}t). (122)

We should emphasize that, according to Eq. (121), the coupling of the nuclear displacements to the electrons is completely defined by the electronic dielectric matrix through WeW_{\rm e}. Similarly, the nuclei affect the electronic structure via the dielectric matrix which enters WphW_{\rm ph} in Eq. (110) and via the nuclear density inside VtotV_{\rm tot} in Eq. (79). From these considerations it should be clear that the electronic dielectric matrix ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) plays an absolutely central role in the the field-theoretic approach to the electron-phonon problem.

IV.4 Hedin-Baym equations

Apart from making use of the harmonic approximation, the set of equations given by Eqs. (79), (84), (85), (87), (92), (93), (94), (95), (110), (118), (121), and (122) describe the coupled electron-phonon system entirely from first principles. This set of equations can be regarded as the most sophisticated description of interacting electrons and phonons available today. Since the self-consistent equations for the electrons were originally derived by Hedin [187], and those for the nuclei were derived first by Baym [46], we will refer to the complete set as the Hedin-Baym equations. Given the importance of these relations, we summarize them schematically in Table 1. The standard Hedin’s equations for interacting electrons in the potential of clamped nuclei [187] are immediately recovered from the Hedin-Baym equations by setting to zero the displacement-displacement correlation function of the nuclei, Dκ​p​α,κ′​p′​α′=0D_{\kappa p{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}=0.

Table 1 provides a closed set of self-consistent equations whose solution yields the Green’s functions of a fully-interacting electron-phonon system, within the harmonic approximation. We stress that these relations are fundamentally different from diagrammatic approaches. In fact, here the coupled electron-phonon system is not addressed using Feynman-Dyson perturbation theory as it was done for example by Keating [216]. Instead, in Table 1, electrons and phonons are described non-perturbatively by means of a coupled set of nonlinear equations for the exact propagators. In particular we emphasize that this approach does not require the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation, and therefore it encompasses insulators, intrinsic as well as doped semiconductors, metals, and superconductors.

Almost every property related to electron-phonon interactions in solids that can be calculated today from first principles can be derived from these equations. Examples to be discussed in Secs. V-X include the renormalization of the Fermi velocity, the band gap renormalization in semiconductors and insulators, the non-adiabatic corrections to vibrational frequencies, the Frölich interaction, and the lifetimes of electrons and phonons. The generalization of these results to the case of finite temperature should also be able to describe phonon-mediated superconductivity, although this phenomenon is best addressed by studying directly the propagation of Cooper pairs (see Sec. XI).

Baym’s theory can in principle be extended to go beyond the harmonic approximation [150]. However, the mathematical complexity of the resulting formalism is formidable, due to the appearance of many additional terms which are neglected in the harmonic approximation.

V From a many-body formalism to practical calculations

The Hedin-Baym equations summarized in Table 1 define a rigorous formalism for studying interacting electrons and phonons in metals, semiconductors, and insulators entirely from first principles. However, a direct numerical solution of these equations for real materials is currently out of reach, and approximations are needed for practical calculations. The following sections establish the connection between the Hedin-Baym equations and standard expressions which are currently in use in ab initio calculations of electron-phonon interactions.

V.1 Effects of the electron-phonon interaction on phonons

V.1.1 Phonons in the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation

The vibrational eigenmodes of the nuclei can be identified with the resonances of the displacement-displacement correlation function Dκ​p​α,κ′​p′​α′​(t​t′)D_{\kappa p{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime}) in the frequency domain. If we denote by 𝐌{\bf M} the diagonal matrix having the nuclear masses MκM_{\kappa} along its diagonal, then the formal solution of Eq. (118) can be written as:

𝐃⁡(ω)=[𝐌​ω2−𝚷⁡(ω)]−1,{\bf D}(\omega)=\left[\,{\bf M}\,\omega^{2}-{\bf\Pi}(\omega)\,\right]^{-1}, (123)

where 𝐃{\bf D} is the matrix with elements Dκ​p​α,κ′​p′​α′D_{\kappa p{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}. The resonant frequencies of the system correspond to the solutions of the nonlinear equations:

Ων(ω)−ω=0,with ν=1,…3M,\Omega_{\nu}(\omega)-\omega=0,\,\,\,\,\,\mbox{with }\nu=1,\dots 3M,\!\!\!\!\!\! (124)

where Ων2​(ω)\Omega^{2}_{\nu}(\omega) is an eigenvalue of 𝐌−1/2𝚷(ω)𝐌−1/2{\bf M}^{-1/2}\,{\bf\Pi}(\omega)\,{\bf M}^{-1/2}, parametric in the variable ω\omega.

As expected, the study of lattice vibrations within a field-theoretic framework resembles the standard eigenvalue problem reviewed in Sec. III.1. In particular, the matrix 𝚷⁡(ω){\bf\Pi}(\omega) represents the many-body counterpart of the matrix of interatomic force constants Cκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′C_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}} introduced in Eq. (13). However, despite its formal simplicity, Eq. (124) conceals the full wealth of information associated with the many-body electronic screening ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) via Eq. (121). In fact, the phonon self-energy is generally complex and frequency-dependent. Therefore we can expect to find roots of Eq. (124) outside of the real frequency axis, as well as multiple roots for the same ‘eigenmode’.

The link between Eq. (124) and phonon calculations by means of DFT is established by noting that DFT relies on the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation. In the adiabatic approximation the nuclei are considered immobile during characteristic electronic timescales. Formally, this approximation is introduced by setting ω=0\omega=0 in Eq. (121) [216]. In practice, this assumption corresponds to stating that ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) can be replaced by ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,0)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},0) in the frequency range of the vibrational excitations. Obviously this is not always the case, and important exceptions will be discussed in Sec. V.1.2.

In order to see more clearly the connection with the formalism discussed in Sec. III.1, we partition the phonon self-energy into ‘adiabatic’ and ‘non-adiabatic’ contributions:

𝚷⁡(ω)=𝚷A+𝚷NA​(ω),{\bf\Pi}(\omega)={\bf\Pi}^{\rm A}+{\bf\Pi}^{\rm NA}(\omega), (125)

with 𝚷A=𝚷⁡(ω=0){\bf\Pi}^{\rm A}={\bf\Pi}(\omega\!=\!0). As we will see below, the adiabatic term 𝚷A{\bf\Pi}^{\rm A} will be taken to describe ‘non-interacting’ phonons, and the non-adiabatic self-energy ΠNA\Pi^{\rm NA} will be used to describe the effects of electron-phonon interactions.

In the early literature it is common to find a different partitioning, whereby the non-interacting system is defined by the bare interatomic force constants, corresponding to nuclei in the absence of electrons [170]. This alternative choice is not useful in modern calculations, because the resulting non-interacting phonon dispersions are very different from the fully-interacting dispersions. The present choice of using instead adiabatic phonons as the non-interacting system, is more convenient in the context of modern ab initio techniques, since calculations of adiabatic phonon spectra are routinely performed within DFPT.

In the remainder of this section we concentrate on the adiabatic term, and we defer the discussion of the non-adiabatic self-energy to Sec. V.1.2. Using Eq. (121), we can rewrite the adiabatic self-energy as follows:

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A=∑κ′′​p′′(δκ′​p′,κ′′​p′′−δκ​p,κ′​p′)\displaystyle\hskip-19.91684pt\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\rm A}=\sum_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}(\delta_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}-\delta_{\kappa p,\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}})
×[∫d​𝐫​∂⟨n^e​(𝐫)⟩∂τκ′′​α′​p′′​∂Ven​(𝐫)∂τκ​α​p+∂2Unn∂τκ​α​p​∂τκ′′​α′​p′′].\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt\times\left[\int\!d{\bf r}\,\frac{\partial\,\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\rangle}{\partial\tau_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}}\frac{\partial V^{\rm en}({\bf r})}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}}+\frac{\partial^{2}U_{\rm nn}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}\partial\tau_{\kappa^{\prime\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime\prime}}}\right]\!\!. (126)

In this expression UnnU_{\rm nn} is the nucleus-nucleus interaction energy from Eq. (65), VenV^{\rm en} is the electron-nuclei interaction from Eq. (25), and all the derivatives are taken at the equilibrium coordinates. The derivation of Eq. (126) requires the use of the identity:

∂⟨n^e​(𝐫)⟩∂τκ​α​p0=−Zκ∫d𝐫′[ϵe−1(𝐫,𝐫′;0)−δ(𝐫,𝐫′)]∇α′δ(𝐫′−𝝉κ​p0).\frac{\partial\,\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\rangle}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}^{0}}\!=-{Z_{\kappa}}\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}[\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime};0)\!-\!\delta({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})]\nabla^{\prime}_{{\alpha}}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}^{0}_{\kappa p}). (127)

This identity follows from the same reasoning leading to Eq. (100), after considering an external potential which modifies the position of the nucleus κ\kappa in the cell pp. Equation (126) can be recast in a familiar form by exploiting the acoustic sum rule in Eq. (120). Indeed after a few tedious but straightforward manipulations we obtain:

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A=∫d​𝐫​∂⟨n^e​(𝐫)⟩∂τκ′​α′​p′​∂Ven​(𝐫)∂τκ​α​p\displaystyle\hskip-22.76228pt\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\rm A}=\int\!d{\bf r}\,\frac{\partial\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\rangle}{\partial\tau_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}}\frac{\partial V^{\rm en}({\bf r})}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}}
+∫d𝐫⟨n^e(𝐫)⟩∂2Ven​(𝐫)∂τκ​α​p​∂τκ′​α′​p′+∂2Unn∂τκ​α​p​∂τκ′​α′​p′.\displaystyle\hskip-2.84544pt+\int\!d{\bf r}\,\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\rangle\frac{\partial^{2}V^{\rm en}({\bf r})}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}\partial\tau_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}}+\frac{\partial^{2}U_{\rm nn}}{\partial\tau_{\kappa{\alpha}p}\partial\tau_{\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}}. (128)

In this form, one can see that the adiabatic self-energy gives precisely the interatomic force constants that we would obtain using the Born-Oppenheimer approximation and the Hellman-Feynman theorem, compare Eq. (128) for example with Baroni et al. (2001, p. 517).

The difference between the Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\rm A} in Eq. (128) and the Cκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′C_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}} in Eq. (13) is that, in the former case, the electron density response to atomic displacements is governed by the exact many-body dielectric matrix ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,0)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},0) and electron density ⟨n^e​(𝐫)⟩\langle{\hat{n}_{\rm e}}({\bf r})\rangle, as shown by Eqs. (127) and (128). As a result, Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\rm A} corresponds to force constants and electron density dressed by all many-body interactions of the system (both electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions). In contrast, when the force constants in Eq. (13) are calculated using DFT, the electron density response to an atomic displacement is evaluated using the RPA+x​cxc screening, that is ϵH​x​c​(𝐫,𝐫′)\epsilon^{{\rm H}xc}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}) from Sec. III.2.4, and the ground-state electron density is calculated at clamped nuclei.

The use of the adiabatic approximation in the study of phonons carries the important advantage that the many-body force constants 𝚷A{\bf\Pi}^{\rm A} form a real and symmetric matrix. This can be seen by rewriting Eq. (121) for ω=0\omega=0, and using the relation We​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=We​(𝐫′,𝐫,−ω)W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)=W_{\rm e}({\bf r}^{\prime},{\bf r},-\omega) which follows from the property W⁡(12)=W⁡(21)W(12)=W(21) (see Sec. IV.2). Since 𝚷A{\bf\Pi}^{\rm A} is real and symmetric, all its eigenvalues are guaranteed to be real. In this approximation, the excitations of the lattice correspond to sharp resonances in the displacement-displacement correlation function 𝐃⁡(ω){\bf D}(\omega), and it is meaningful to talk about phonons as long-lived excitations of the system. In fact these excitations are infinitely long-lived in the harmonic approximation. In practical calculations, the many-body 𝚷A{\bf\Pi}^{\rm A} is invariably replaced by the DFT interatomic force constants, and in this case the agreement of the calculated phonon frequencies with experiment is excellent in most cases. Illustrative examples can be found among others in (Yin and Cohen, 1982; Giannozzi et al., 1991; Dal Corso et al., 1993; Lee et al., 1994; Kresse et al., 1995; Dal Corso and de Gironcoli, 2000; Bungaro et al., 2000; Karki et al., 2000; Baroni et al., 2001; Díaz-Sánchez et al., 2007; Dal Corso, 2013).

The most obvious criticism to the adiabatic approximation is that, in the case of metals, the assumption ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)≃ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,0)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)\!\simeq\!\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},0) is inadequate. This can intuitively be understood by recalling that the dielectric function of the homogeneous electron gas diverges when ω,𝐪→0\omega,{\bf q}\!\rightarrow\!0 [267]. In practical calculations, this divergence is connected with vanishing denominators in Eq. (51) for 𝐪→0{\bf q}\!\rightarrow\!0. An approximate, yet very successful strategy for overcoming this problem, is to replace the occupation numbers in Eq. (51) by smoothing functions such as the Fermi-Dirac distribution, and to describe the singular terms analytically [151]. Most first-principles calculations of phonon dispersion relations in metals have been carried out using this strategy. Improvements upon this strategy will be discussed in Sec. V.1.2.

The adiabatic approximation leads naturally to the definition of an ‘adiabatic’ propagator 𝐃A​(ω){\bf D}^{\rm A}(\omega), which can be obtained from Eq. (123) after replacing the phonon self-energy by its static limit:

𝐃A​(ω)=[𝐌​ω2−𝚷A]−1.{\bf D}^{\rm A}(\omega)=\left[\,{\bf M}\,\omega^{2}-{\bf\Pi}^{\rm A}\,\right]^{-1}. (129)

Now, if we identify Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A\Pi_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{\rm A} with the interatomic force constant Cκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′C_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}} in Eq. (13), we can obtain an explicit expression for the adiabatic phonon propagator in terms of the eigenmodes eκ​α,ν​(𝐪)e_{\kappa{\alpha},\nu}({\bf q}) and eigenfrequencies ω𝐪​ν\omega_{{\bf q}\nu} introduced in Sec. III.1. To this end we invert Eq. (129) using Eqs. (14)-(17), and recall that the dynamical matrix is Hermitian and obeys the relation Dκ​α,κ′​α′dm,∗​(𝐪)=Dκ​α,κ′​α′dm​(−𝐪)D^{{\rm dm},*}_{\kappa{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}({\bf q})=D_{\kappa{\alpha},\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}}^{\rm dm}(-{\bf q}) [271]. After tedious but straightforward steps we find:

Dκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′A​(ω)=∑ν∫d​𝐪ΩBZ​S𝐪​ν,κ​α​p∗​S𝐪​ν,κ′​α′​p′​2​ω𝐪​νω2−ω𝐪​ν2,D^{\rm A}_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega)={\sum}_{\nu}\!\!\int\!\!\frac{d{\bf q}}{\Omega_{\rm BZ}}\,S^{*}_{{\bf q}\nu,\kappa{\alpha}p}S_{{\bf q}\nu,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}\,\frac{2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}}{\omega^{2}-\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2}}, (130)

with the definition:

S𝐪​ν,κ​α​p=ei​𝐪⋅𝐑p(2Mκω𝐪​ν)−1/2eκ​α,ν(𝐪).S_{{\bf q}\nu,\kappa{\alpha}p}=e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf R}_{p}}(2M_{\kappa}\omega_{{\bf q}\nu})^{-1/2}\,e_{\kappa{\alpha},\nu}({\bf q}). (131)

This result suggests that, as expected, the propagator should take a simple form in the eigenmodes representation. In fact, by using the inverse transform of Eq. (131) we have: D𝐪​ν,𝐪′​ν′A​(ω)=ΩBZ​δ​(𝐪−𝐪′)​D𝐪​ν​ν′A​(ω),D^{\rm A}_{{\bf q}\nu,{\bf q}^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}(\omega)=\Omega_{\rm BZ}\,\delta({\bf q}\!-\!{\bf q}^{\prime})D^{\rm A}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}(\omega), with

D𝐪​ν​ν′A​(ω)=2​ω𝐪​ν/(ω2−ω𝐪​ν2)​δν​ν′.\displaystyle D^{\rm A}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}(\omega)=2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}/(\omega^{2}-\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2})\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}. (132)

This result can alternatively be obtained starting from the ladder operators of Appendix B. In fact, after using Eqs. (20), (109), and (131) we find:

D𝐪​ν​ν′A​(t​t′)=−i⁡⟨T^​[a^𝐪​ν†​(t)​a^𝐪​ν​(t′)+a^−𝐪​ν​(t)​a^−𝐪​ν†​(t′)]⟩​δν​ν′.D^{\rm A}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}(tt^{\prime})=-i\langle{\hat{T}}\,[{\hat{a}}^{\dagger}_{{\bf q}\nu}(t){\hat{a}}_{{\bf q}\nu}(t^{\prime})+{\hat{a}}_{-{\bf q}\nu}(t){\hat{a}}^{\dagger}_{-{\bf q}\nu}(t^{\prime})]\rangle\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}. (133)

An explicit evaluation of the right-hand side using the Heisenberg time evolution generated by the phonon Hamiltonian in Eq. (22) yields precisely Eq. (132), with the added advantage that it is easier to keep track of the time-ordering. The result is:

D𝐪​ν​νA​(ω)=1ω−ω𝐪​ν+i​η−1ω+ω𝐪​ν−i​η,D^{\rm A}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega-\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}+i\eta}-\frac{1}{\omega+\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}-i\eta}, (134)

with η\eta a positive real infinitesimal. This alternative approach is very common in textbooks, see for example Schrieffer [363] and Schäfer and Wegener [362]. However, it does not carry general validity in a field-theoretic framework since it rests on the adiabatic approximation.

V.1.2 Phonons beyond the adiabatic approximation

In order to go beyond the adiabatic approximation, it is necessary to determine the complete propagator 𝐃⁡(ω){\bf D}(\omega) in Eq. (123). Formally this can be done by combining Eqs. (123) and (125) to obtain the following Dyson-like equation:

𝐃⁡(ω)=𝐃A​(ω)+𝐃A​(ω)​𝚷NA​(ω)​𝐃​(ω).{\bf D}(\omega)={\bf D}^{\rm A}(\omega)+{\bf D}^{\rm A}(\omega){\bf\Pi}^{\rm NA}(\omega){\bf D}(\omega). (135)

In this form it is apparent that the non-adiabatic phonon self-energy 𝚷NA​(ω){\bf\Pi}^{\rm NA}(\omega) ‘dresses’ the non-interacting phonons obtained within the adiabatic approximation, as shown schematically in Fig. 1(a). It is convenient to rewrite the Dyson equation in such a way as to show more clearly the poles of the propagator. Using Eqs. (131)-(132) we find:

D𝐪​ν​ν′−1​(ω)=12​ω𝐪​ν​[δν​ν′​(ω2−ω𝐪​ν2)−2​ω𝐪​ν​Π𝐪​ν​ν′NA​(ω)],D^{-1}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}(\omega)=\frac{1}{2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}}\left[\delta_{\nu\nu^{\prime}}(\omega^{2}-\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2})-2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}^{\rm NA}(\omega)\right], (136)

where Π𝐪​ν​ν′NA\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}^{\rm NA} and D𝐪​ν​ν′−1D^{-1}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}} are obtained using the transform of Eq. (131) and its inverse, respectively.

From Eq. (136) we see that the non-adiabatic self-energy ΠNA\Pi^{\rm NA} modifies the adiabatic phonon spectrum in four distinct ways: (i) the real part of the diagonal elements Π𝐪​ν​νNA\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA} shifts the adiabatic frequencies; (ii) the imaginary part introduces spectral broadening; (iii) the off-diagonal elements of Π𝐪​ν​ν′NA\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu^{\prime}}^{\rm NA} introduce a coupling between the adiabatic vibrational eigenmodes; (iv) the frequency-dependence of Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(ω)\Pi^{\rm NA}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}(\omega) might lead to multiple poles for the same mode ν\nu, thereby introducing new structures in the phonon spectrum.

Today it is relatively common to calculate phonon linewidths arising from electron-phonon interactions [12, 45]. Recently it has also become possible to study the frequency renormalization due to non-adiabatic effects [350, 70].

The possibility of observing new features in vibrational spectra arising from the EPI has not been studied from first principles, but the underlying phenomenology should be similar to that of plasmon satellites in photoelectron spectra (see Sec. V.2.6). Generally speaking we expect satellites whenever ϵe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\epsilon_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) exhibits dynamical structure close to vibrational frequencies. This can happen, for example, in the case of degenerate polar semicondutors, when phonon and plasmon energies are in resonance. In these cases, phonons and plasmons can combine into ‘coupled plasmon-phonon modes’ [345], which are the electronic analogue of photon polaritons (Yu and Cardona, 2010, p. 295). This phenomenon was predicted theoretically [385], and subsequently confirmed by Raman measurements on GaAs [293]. We speculate that it should be possible to obtain coupled plasmon-phonon modes from the frequency-dependence of the phonon self-energy in Eq. (136); it would be interesting to perform first-principles calculations in order to shed light on these aspects.

In practical calculations the non-adiabatic corrections to the adiabatic phonon spectrum are evaluated from Eq. (136) using first-order perturbation theory, by retaining only the diagonal elements of ΠNA\Pi^{\rm NA}. If we denote the complex zeros of D𝐪​ν​ν−1​(ω)D^{-1}_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}(\omega) by Ω~𝐪​ν=Ω𝐪​ν−i​γ𝐪​ν\tilde{\Omega}_{{\bf q}\nu}=\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}-i\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}, in the case of non-degenerate eigenmodes Eq. (136) gives:

Ω~𝐪​ν2=ω𝐪​ν2+2​ω𝐪​ν​Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(Ω~𝐪​ν),\tilde{\Omega}_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2}=\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2}+2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA}(\tilde{\Omega}_{{\bf q}\nu}), (137)

therefore:

γ𝐪​ν\displaystyle\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu} =\displaystyle= −ω𝐪​νΩ𝐪​ν​Im​Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(Ω𝐪​ν−i​γ𝐪​ν),\displaystyle-\frac{\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}}{\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}}{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA}(\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}-i\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}), (138)
Ω𝐪​ν2\displaystyle\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2} =\displaystyle= ω𝐪​ν2+γ𝐪​ν2+2​ω𝐪​ν​Re​Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(Ω𝐪​ν−i​γ𝐪​ν).\displaystyle\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2}+\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2}+2\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}{\rm Re}\,\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA}(\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}-i\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}).\,\,\, (139)

Apart from the small γ𝐪​ν2\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}^{2} term in the second line, these expressions are identical to those provided by Allen [12] and Grimvall [170]. Since non-adiabatic corrections are usually small as compared to the adiabatic phonon frequencies, the above expressions are often simplified further by using the additional approximations |Ω𝐪​ν−ω𝐪​ν|≪ω𝐪​ν|\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}-\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}|\ll\omega_{{\bf q}\nu} and |γ𝐪​ν|≪ω𝐪​ν|\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}|\ll\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}, leading to γ𝐪​ν≃−Im​Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(ω𝐪​ν)\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu}\simeq-{\rm Im}\,\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA}(\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}) and Ω𝐪​ν≃ω𝐪​ν+Re​Π𝐪​ν​νNA​(ω𝐪​ν)\Omega_{{\bf q}\nu}\simeq\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}+{\rm Re}\,\Pi_{{\bf q}\nu\nu}^{\rm NA}(\omega_{{\bf q}\nu}). In these forms it becomes evident that the real part of the self-energy shifts the adiabatic phonon frequencies, and the imaginary part is responsible for the spectral broadening of the resonances. Using these expressions in Eq. (136) and going back to the time domain, it is seen that, as a result of the EPI, phonons acquire a finite lifetime given by τ𝐪​νph=(2​γ𝐪​ν)−1\tau^{\rm ph}_{{\bf q}\nu}=(2\gamma_{{\bf q}\nu})^{-1}.

V.1.3 Expressions for the phonon self-energy used in ab initio calculations

In the literature on electron-phonon interactions, the phonon self-energy Π\Pi is almost invariably expressed in terms of an electron-phonon vertex gg and the electron Green’s function GG as Π=|g|2​G​G\Pi=|g|^{2}GG in symbolic notation, see for example Grimvall (1981, p. 195). While this has become common practice also in ab initio calculations, the origin of this choice is not entirely transparent. One could derive the above expression directly from Eq. (1), using standard Green’s function techniques. However, this procedure does not answer the key question on how to calculate the electron-phonon matrix elements gg.

Closer inspection of the theory reveals that this is a rather nontrivial point. In fact, on the one hand, a straightforward expansion of the second-quantized Hamiltonian of Eq. (68) in terms of the nuclear coordinates leads to ‘bare’ electron-phonon matrix elements, gbg^{\rm b}, which contain the bare Coulomb interaction between electrons and nuclei. On the other hand, if we go back to Sec. III.2.2, we see that the electron-phonon matrix elements in DFT are ‘dressed’ by the self-consistent response of the electrons. The difference between bare and dressed vertex is not only quantitative, but also qualitative: for example in metals the bare vertex is long-ranged, while the screened vertex is short-ranged.

The relation between bare and dressed electron-phonon vertices and the derivation of explicit expressions for the phonon self-energy have been discussed by many authors, see for example Scalapino [361], Rickayzen [346]. In short the argument is that the lowest-order Feynman diagram starting and ending with a phonon line must contain precisely two bare electron-phonon vertices, as shown in Fig. 1(b). By construction this diagram corresponds to having Π=|gb|2​G​G\Pi=|g^{\rm b}|^{2}GG. In order to make the transition from the bare vertex to the dressed vertex it is necessary to collect together all the proper electronic polarization diagrams around the vertex. However, these steps have been carried out only for the homogeneous electron gas [361, 346]. In the following we show how the dressed electron-phonon vertex emerges from a non-perturbative analysis based on the Hedin-Baym equations.

The non-adiabatic phonon self-energy ΠNA\Pi^{\rm NA} introduced in Sec. V.1.2 can be written explicitly by combining Eqs. (119) and (125):

Πκ​α​p,κ′​α′​p′NA​(ω)=∫d​𝐫​d​𝐫′​Zκ​∇αδ​(𝐫−𝝉κ​p0)\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\Pi^{\rm NA}_{\kappa{\alpha}p,\kappa^{\prime}{\alpha}^{\prime}p^{\prime}}(\omega)=\int\!\!d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}Z_{\kappa}\nabla_{\!{\alpha}}\,\delta({\bf r}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa p}^{0})
×[We​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)−We​(𝐫,𝐫′,0)]​Zκ′​∇α′′δ​(𝐫′−𝝉κ′​p′0).\displaystyle\hskip-8.5359pt\times\left[W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)-W_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},0)\right]Z_{\kappa^{\prime}}\nabla^{\prime}_{\!{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta({\bf r}^{\prime}\!-\!{\bm{\tau}}_{\kappa^{\prime}p^{\prime}}^{0}). (140)

Using the Dyson equation for the screened Coulomb interaction, it can be seen that this expression does indeed contain electron-phonon matrix elements. In fact, by inserting Eq. (94) into Eq. (140) we find terms like v​Pe​WevP_{\rm e}W_{\rm e}, and the electron-phonon matrix elements will arise from taking the gradients of vv and WeW_{\rm e}, respectively. By working in the eigenmodes representation via Eq. (131), after lengthy manipulations this procedure yields:

ℏ​Π𝐪​ν,𝐪′​ν′NA​(ω)\displaystyle\hskip-17.07182pt\hbar\,\Pi^{\rm NA}_{{\bf q}\nu,{\bf q}^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}(\omega) =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐫​d​𝐫′​g𝐪​νb​(𝐫)​Pe​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)​g𝐪′​ν′cc​(𝐫′,ω)\displaystyle\!\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,g^{\rm b}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r})P_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)\,g^{\rm cc}_{{\bf q}^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}({\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) (141)
−\displaystyle- ∫d​𝐫​d​𝐫′​g𝐪​νb​(𝐫)​Pe​(𝐫,𝐫′, 0)​g𝐪′​ν′∗​(𝐫′,0),\displaystyle\!\!\int\!\!d{\bf r}d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,g^{\rm b}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r})P_{\rm e}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\,0)\,g^{*}_{{\bf q}^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}({\bf r}^{\prime},\hskip 0.9pt0),\,\,\,\,

where we introduced electron-phonon ‘coupling functions’ as follows. The bare coupling gbg^{\rm b} is defined as:

g𝐪​νb​(𝐫)=Δ𝐪​ν​Ven​(𝐫),g^{\rm b}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r})=\Delta_{{\bf q}\nu}V^{\rm en}({\bf r}), (142)

where VenV^{\rm en} is the potential of the nuclei from Eq. (25); in practical calculations this quantity is replaced by the usual ionic pseudo-potentials. The meaning of the variation Δ𝐪​ν\Delta_{{\bf q}\nu} is the same as in Eqs. (33)-(35). The dressed couplings gg and gccg^{\rm cc} are defined as [189]:

g𝐪​ν​(𝐫,ω)\displaystyle g_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r},\omega) =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐫′​ϵe−1​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)​g𝐪​νb​(𝐫′),\displaystyle\int\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)\,g^{\rm b}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r}^{\prime}), (143)
g𝐪​νcc​(𝐫,ω)\displaystyle g^{\rm cc}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r},\omega) =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐫′​ϵe−1​(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)​g𝐪​νb,∗​(𝐫′).\displaystyle\int\!d{\bf r}^{\prime}\,\epsilon_{\rm e}^{-1}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)\,g^{\rm b,*}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r}^{\prime}). (144)

Since the dielectric matrix is real at ω=0\omega\!=\!0, we have the simple relation g𝐪​νcc​(𝐫,0)=g𝐪​ν∗​(𝐫,0)g^{\rm cc}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r},0)\!=\!g^{*}_{{\bf q}\nu}({\bf r},0).
